question: What mainly dictates the initial design of an instrument approach procedure?

options.text: The airline that will use it most
The terrain surrounding the aerodrome
The direction of the prevailing wind in winter months at the aerodrome
The number of runways available

explanation: Approach design is dictated mainly by the surrounding terrain, and also by the type of operations, aircraft types and airspace restrictions.

question: A pilot reports being unfamiliar with an instrument approach procedure. What must ATC do?

options.text: Describe the procedure, unless the aircraft is cleared for a straight-in approach
Clear the aircraft for a visual approach instead
Ask the operator to send the chart to the aircraft by data link before it starts the approach
Refuse the approach and divert the aircraft

explanation: ATC is responsible for describing the procedure to an unfamiliar pilot, unless the aircraft is cleared straight-in (when only the final approach track need be given).

question: The threshold speed Vat used to categorise aircraft for approach is based on:

options.text: The maximum flap extension speed
1.3 × VS0 at the mass expected at the destination on the day of the flight
1.3 VS0 (or 1.23 VS1g), landing configuration, max landing mass
1.2 × VS1 at the actual landing mass

explanation: Vat is 1.3 × stall speed in landing configuration (VS0) or 1.23 × VS1g, at maximum certificated landing mass.

question: An aircraft has a Vat of 135 kt. Which approach category is it?

options.text: D
E
B
C

explanation: Categories by Vat: A below 91 kt, B 91–120, C 121–140, D 141–165, E 166–210.

question: An aircraft has a Vat of 118 kt. Which approach category is it?

options.text: C
D
A
B

explanation: Category B covers Vat 91 to 120 kt.

question: For a Category A aircraft, the speed range for the initial approach is:

options.text: 120 to 180 kt
90 to 150 kt
70 to 100 kt
160 to 240 kt

explanation: Initial approach speed ranges: A 90–150 kt, B 120–180 kt, C 160–240 kt, D and E 185–250 kt.

question: What is the maximum speed for a Category B aircraft flying a reversal or racetrack procedure?

options.text: 110 kt
135 kt
140 kt
180 kt

explanation: The maximum speed for reversal and racetrack procedures is 110 kt for Category A and 140 kt for Category B.

question: The final approach speed range for a Category D aircraft is:

options.text: 130 to 185 kt
155 to 230 kt
115 to 160 kt
185 to 250 kt

explanation: Final approach speed ranges: A 70–100, B 85–130, C 115–160, D 130–185, E 155–230 kt.

question: What is the maximum speed for visual manoeuvring (circling) for a Category C aircraft?

options.text: 135 kt
180 kt
205 kt
160 kt

explanation: Maximum circling speeds: A 100, B 135, C 180, D 205, E 240 kt.

question: The minimum sector altitude (or terminal arrival altitude) gives an obstacle clearance of at least:

options.text: 600 m (1969 ft) within 25 NM of the navaid
300 m (984 ft) within 10 NM of the aerodrome
150 m (492 ft) within 25 NM of the aerodrome reference point
300 m (984 ft) within 25 NM of the navaid, IAF or IF

explanation: MSA/TAA provides at least 300 m (984 ft) obstacle clearance within 25 NM of the navaid, IAF or IF associated with the approaches.

question: An arriving aircraft may descend below the MSA when:

options.text: ATC has passed the latest QNH and the transition level and the aircraft is within 25 NM
It is within 10 NM of the aerodrome
It is radar vectored, or flying the published approach, or has the terrain in sight
It is in VMC above cloud

explanation: Descent below MSA is permitted only with the aerodrome and terrain visible (and remaining so), when radar vectored, or when flying a published approach procedure.

question: A precision approach procedure provides:

options.text: Track guidance in azimuth and information on height above the threshold
Azimuth guidance only, with distance information
Guidance only until the final approach fix
Elevation guidance only, with the pilot following the runway lights for azimuth

explanation: A precision approach gives track guidance (azimuth) and height (elevation) information in the final segment; ILS, MLS and PAR are examples.

question: On a precision approach, what deviation must the pilot stay within to remain inside the protected area?

options.text: One dot on the glide path only
Quarter-scale deflection in azimuth only, with any deviation in elevation acceptable
Full-scale deflection
Half-scale deflection of the course deviation indicator

explanation: Flying the track and glide path within half-scale CDI deflection keeps the aircraft within the protected area above OCA/H.

question: On a precision approach, the pilot reaches the DA/H without the required visual reference. What must happen?

options.text: The autopilot must be disconnected for a manual landing, whether or not the runway is in sight
The aircraft may descend a further 100 ft to look for the lights
A missed approach must be started
The pilot must report to ATC and continue to the minimum descent height

explanation: DA/H is the specified altitude/height in a precision approach at which a missed approach must be initiated if the required visual reference to continue has not been established.

question: During an ILS approach, the glide path becomes unserviceable. What type of approach does it become?

options.text: A non-precision approach
A circling approach
A visual approach
It remains a precision approach using DME heights

explanation: Without glide path indications, the approach becomes a non-precision (localizer) approach.

question: The minima for a CAT I precision approach are a DH not lower than 200 ft and:

options.text: An RVR not less than 175 m
A visibility not less than 800 m or an RVR not less than 550 m
A visibility not less than 1500 m and an RVR not less than 800 m
An RVR not less than 300 m

explanation: CAT I: DH not lower than 60 m (200 ft) and either visibility not less than 800 m or RVR not less than 550 m.

question: A CAT II precision approach has a decision height:

options.text: Lower than 200 ft but not lower than 100 ft, with an RVR not less than 300 m
Not lower than 200 ft, with an RVR not less than 550 m
Lower than 100 ft, with an RVR not less than 175 m
Lower than 200 ft but not lower than 50 ft, with a runway visual range of not less than 200 m

explanation: CAT II: DH below 60 m (200 ft) but not lower than 30 m (100 ft), RVR not less than 300 m.

question: A CAT IIIA precision approach has:

options.text: No DH and no RVR limitations
A DH lower than 100 ft or no DH, and an RVR not less than 175 m
A DH lower than 50 ft or no DH, and an RVR less than 175 m but not less than 50 m
A DH lower than 200 ft, and an RVR not less than 300 m

explanation: CAT IIIA: DH below 30 m (100 ft) or no DH, RVR not less than 175 m.

question: A CAT IIIB precision approach has:

options.text: A DH lower than 50 ft or no DH, and a runway visual range of not less than 300 m
No DH and no RVR limitations
A DH lower than 50 ft or no DH, and an RVR less than 175 m but not less than 50 m
A DH lower than 100 ft, and an RVR not less than 175 m

explanation: CAT IIIB: DH below 15 m (50 ft) or no DH, RVR less than 175 m but not less than 50 m.

question: A CAT IIIC precision approach has:

options.text: No DH and an RVR not less than 50 m
A DH of 0 ft with an RVR not less than 75 m for taxiing
A DH of 50 ft and an RVR of 50 m
No DH and no RVR limitations

explanation: CAT IIIC: no DH and no RVR limitations.

question: Which approach is non-precision?

options.text: A PAR approach
An MLS approach with elevation guidance available
An ILS localizer-only approach
An ILS approach with the glide path working

explanation: Non-precision approaches lack elevation guidance: VOR, NDB, localizer only, PAR azimuth only or surveillance radar. They terminate above touchdown and are sometimes called aerodrome approaches.

question: After establishing visual reference on final, the pilot continues an instrument approach visually. Who provides separation?

options.text: ATC, because other aircraft may be flying instrument approaches
The pilot alone, as the flight is now VFR
The tower only, for the last two miles, once the pilot has reported the runway in sight
Nobody, until the aircraft lands

explanation: Continuing the IFR procedure visually is not VFR; separation remains ATC's responsibility since other aircraft may be on instrument approaches.

question: Once an instrument approach procedure has been started, the pilot must:

options.text: Fly it only as far as the final approach fix
Change to VFR when in visual contact with the ground, telling ATC the IFR flight is cancelled
Abandon it as soon as the runway is in sight
Complete it as published unless ATC gives other instructions

explanation: Once started, a procedure is completed as published unless ATC instructs otherwise; even if the final is flown visually, the procedure's requirements still apply.

question: An instrument approach is abandoned after the aircraft has passed the IAF. What should the pilot fly?

options.text: A visual circuit to land
The missed approach procedure, from the missed approach point
A turn back to the IAF at the procedure altitude, followed by a second approach
A direct climb to the cruising level

explanation: If the procedure is abandoned after the IAF, the published missed approach is flown, starting from the MAPt, climbing to the specified altitude as soon as possible.

question: Under the approach ban, a non-precision approach may not be continued below what height above the aerodrome unless the reported visibility or RVR is above the minimum?

options.text: The MDH for the procedure

explanation: A precision approach may not continue beyond the outer marker (or equivalent), and a non-precision approach below 300 m (1000 ft) above the aerodrome, unless the reported visibility/RVR is above minimum.

question: After passing the outer marker on an ILS, the reported RVR falls below the minimum. What may the pilot do?

options.text: Must level off and hold until the RVR improves
Continue to DA/H and land if the required visual reference is then obtained
Must go around immediately
Continue only if the autopilot is engaged and coupled for an automatic landing on that runway

explanation: If the visibility/RVR falls below minimum after the outer marker (or below 1000 ft on a non-precision approach), the approach may be continued to DA/H or MDA/H.

question: Instrument approach procedures depict:

options.text: Headings to fly, without wind correction
Magnetic headings corrected for the forecast wind
Tracks that ATC will correct with radar vectors for the wind on the day of the flight
Tracks to be made good, so the pilot must correct for wind

explanation: Procedures define tracks to be made good (still-air tracks); pilots make allowance for wind.

question: How many separate segments make up an instrument approach procedure?

options.text: Five: arrival, initial, intermediate, final and missed approach
Four: arrival, initial, final and missed approach
Six: arrival, holding, initial, intermediate, final and missed approach
Three: initial, intermediate and final

explanation: An approach has five segments: arrival, initial, intermediate, final and missed approach.

question: How are the segments of an approach procedure normally delimited?

options.text: By time from the IAF
By the change of frequency from approach to tower, or by time from the IAF where no fix exists
By altitude only
Each begins and ends at a designated fix, or a specified point if no fix exists

explanation: Each segment begins and ends at a designated fix; where none is available, a specified point (e.g. the FAP where the glide path is intercepted) may be used.

question: For a non-precision approach to be called straight-in, the final approach track may converge with the runway centreline at an angle of:

options.text: 45° or less
5° or less
30° or less
15° or less

explanation: A non-precision final approach track may converge with the runway heading at 30° or less and still be straight-in.

question: When terrain or other restrictions prevent a straight-in approach, which is specified?

options.text: A circling approach
A visual approach only
A precision approach
A radar approach with a higher minimum

explanation: If a straight-in approach is precluded, a circling approach is specified.

question: An aircraft is considered established on an NDB final approach track when within:

options.text: ±5° of the final approach track
±15° of the published final approach track

explanation: Being established on an NDB means being within 5° either side of the final approach track.

question: In the cross-section of each segment, full obstacle clearance is applied:

options.text: Only in the secondary areas
Over the primary area, reducing to zero at the outer edges of the secondary areas
Equally across the whole protected area
Over the primary area only, with no secondary areas either side of the nominal track

explanation: Each segment has a primary area (full MOC) and secondary areas where MOC reduces to zero at the outer edges.

question: Why is a 75 MHz marker used where an accurate "on top" fix is needed, rather than a VOR?

options.text: A VOR does not work below 1000 ft
A VOR gives poor track guidance
A VOR gives a poor overhead indication because of its cone of confusion
A VOR overhead indication is accurate but cannot be identified by its Morse code near the station

explanation: A VOR gives accurate track guidance but a poor "on top" indication due to the cone of confusion; an NDB is better on top but worse in track. A 75 MHz marker is designed for an accurate overhead fix.

question: For an intersection fix, the assumed bearing accuracy of a VOR radial is:
explanation: For fix tolerance, VOR ±4.5° and ILS localizer ±1.4° are assumed.

question: The assumed track guidance accuracy of an NDB is:
explanation: Track guidance accuracy: VOR ±5.2°, ILS localizer ±2.4°, NDB ±6.9°.

question: The assumed fix tolerance of DME is:

options.text: ±0.25 NM at all distances, without a range-dependent element
±0.5 NM plus 3% of the distance
±0.25 NM (0.46 km) plus 1.25% of the distance to the antenna
±1.25 NM at any range

explanation: DME fix tolerance is ±0.46 km (0.25 NM) + 1.25% of the distance to the antenna.

question: A terminal area surveillance radar fix within 20 NM has an assumed tolerance of:

options.text: ±2 NM

explanation: Terminal area radar within 20 NM: ±1.5 km (0.8 NM); en-route radar within 40 NM: ±3.1 km (1.7 NM).

question: The arrival segment begins where the aircraft:

options.text: Is first given an approach clearance by ATC, whatever its position on the route
Passes the initial approach fix
Reaches the minimum sector altitude
Leaves the en-route airway system to begin the instrument arrival

explanation: The arrival segment begins where the aircraft leaves the en-route structure; en-route MOC applies and aircraft are often radar vectored.

question: The initial approach segment runs from the IAF to the IF and provides a minimum obstacle clearance of:
explanation: In the initial segment the MOC is 300 m (984 ft).

question: In the initial segment, the maximum angle of interception of the intermediate track for a precision approach is:
explanation: Track guidance in the initial segment normally has a maximum intercept angle of 90° for precision approaches and 120° for non-precision approaches.

question: If no track guidance is available to the IF, a dead reckoning segment may be specified, limited to:

options.text: An intercept angle of 30° and a length of 20 NM
An intercept angle of no more than 45° and a length of no more than 10 NM
An intercept angle of 90° and a length of 5 NM
An intercept angle of no more than 30° and a length of no more than 20 NM

explanation: A DR segment must intercept the intermediate track at no more than 45° and be no more than 10 NM long.

question: The intermediate segment is mainly used to:

options.text: Adjust speed and configuration for the final approach, with minimal descent
Hold until the expected approach time
Intercept the glide path from above
Descend rapidly to the minimum descent altitude before the final approach fix is reached

explanation: The intermediate segment (IF to FAF) adjusts speed and configuration; descent is kept to a minimum. MOC reduces from 300 m to 150 m.

question: For a non-precision approach with a FAF, where does the final segment start and end?

options.text: At the IAF, ending at the MDA
At the FAP, ending at the runway
At the IF, ending at the runway threshold or the MDA, whichever comes first
At the FAF, ending at the missed approach point

explanation: With a FAF, the non-precision final segment runs from the FAF to the MAPt.

question: What is the optimum distance of the FAF from the threshold for a non-precision approach?

options.text: 3 NM, with a maximum of 5 NM
4 NM, with a maximum of 7 NM
10 NM, with a maximum of 15 NM
5 NM, with a maximum of 10 NM

explanation: The FAF is optimally 5 NM from the threshold, maximum 10 NM.

question: The optimum descent gradient on a non-precision final approach is about:

options.text: 200 ft/NM (about 2°)
300 ft/NM (about 3°)
500 ft/NM (about 5°)
400 ft/NM (about 4°)

explanation: The required descent gradient should be about 300 ft per NM, approximately 3°.

question: A step-down fix is included in a non-precision final segment. What is published?

options.text: A higher MSA for the procedure
A single OCA/H for the whole segment
Two OCA/H values: one with the step-down fix and one without
A decision height instead of an MDH, as the step-down fix gives vertical guidance

explanation: A step-down fix may be incorporated for obstacle clearance, in which case two OCA/H values are published.

question: On a non-precision approach without a FAF, when may descent to MDA/H begin?

options.text: When the aircraft is established inbound on the final approach track
After a timed outbound leg of one minute from the facility, before the procedure turn
Immediately overhead the facility
Only when the runway is in sight

explanation: Without a FAF (one facility serving as IAF and MAPt), descent to MDA/H is made once established inbound on the final approach track.

question: For an ILS approach, the final segment begins at the final approach point (FAP), which is where:

options.text: The intermediate approach altitude intercepts the nominal glide path
The aircraft reaches 1000 ft above the threshold
The aircraft passes the outer marker
The localizer is first captured and the aircraft is established within half-scale deflection

explanation: The FAP is the point on the localizer where the intermediate approach altitude intercepts the nominal glide path.

question: The FAP on a 3° glide path normally lies between which heights?

options.text: 1500 ft and 2500 ft, about 5 to 8 NM from touchdown
500 ft and 1500 ft, about 2 to 5 NM from touchdown
3000 ft and 5000 ft, about 10 to 16 NM from touchdown
1000 ft and 3000 ft, about 3 to 10 NM from touchdown

explanation: The FAP can be between 300 m (1000 ft) and 900 m (3000 ft), i.e. 3 to 10 NM from touchdown on a 3° (300 ft/NM) glide path.

question: During the final segment of an ILS approach, what is provided so the pilot can verify the glide path information?

options.text: A radar check by the approach controller, who passes the aircraft's height above the threshold
A second glide path transmitter
A fix (e.g. outer marker or DME) at which glide path indications can be checked
A PAPI at the final approach fix

explanation: A fix is specified on the final segment where the glide path information can be verified.

question: Which advantage of a stabilized (constant) descent approach is given?

options.text: No need for any ATC separation or wake turbulence spacing on the final approach
Less noise and fuel, and easier avoidance of wake turbulence from preceding aircraft
Lower decision heights for all aircraft
Higher approach speeds and shorter flight times

explanation: A constant descent from the IAF reduces noise and fuel, and keeping above the preceding aircraft helps avoid wake turbulence.

question: OCA/H is established by the State as:

options.text: The operator's chosen decision height
The aerodrome elevation plus 200 ft
The height of the dominant obstacle plus the minimum obstacle clearance, by aircraft category
The height of the highest obstacle within 25 NM plus 1000 ft, the same for all aircraft categories

explanation: OCA/H is the altitude/height at or above which the aircraft must fly to avoid the dominant obstacle: obstacle height plus MOC. It is published by aircraft category.

question: What is the relationship between OCA/H and the DA/H or MDA/H that may be used?

options.text: OCA/H is the lowest the DA/H or MDA/H can be
OCA/H is used only for circling approaches
DA/H may be lower than OCA/H for CAT I
MDA/H is always 100 ft below OCA/H, to allow for altimeter error

explanation: OCA/H is the lowest that the DA/H or MDA/H can be; operators may add a margin.

question: For a precision approach, the reference datum for OCH and DH is:

options.text: The touchdown zone elevation or aerodrome elevation, whichever is higher
Mean sea level
The aerodrome elevation
The threshold elevation of the landing runway

explanation: For precision approaches the reference datum is always the threshold of the landing runway.

question: For a non-precision approach, the reference datum for OCH is the aerodrome elevation, unless the threshold is more than how far below it?

options.text: 2 m (7 ft)

explanation: Non-precision OCH refers to aerodrome elevation, or threshold elevation if the threshold is more than 2 m (7 ft) below the aerodrome elevation.

question: OCH for visual manoeuvring (circling) is referenced to:

options.text: Mean sea level
The threshold of the runway of the instrument approach
The highest obstacle in the approach area
The aerodrome elevation

explanation: Circling OCA/H is the lowest altitude/height above aerodrome elevation, based on the highest obstacle in the circling area.

question: How does an operator set its decision height for an approach?

options.text: Published OCA/H plus an operator margin, which may be zero
MSA minus 1000 ft for precision approaches
Published OCA/H minus 50 ft, as the published value already contains a large margin
Always 200 ft above the threshold

explanation: The operator determines DA/H or MDA/H from the published OCA/H plus an upper margin (which may be zero), considering crew, aircraft, runway, aids and other factors.

question: What is the system minimum for a CAT I ILS?

options.text: 0 ft

explanation: ILS system minima: CAT I 60 m (200 ft); CAT II 30 m (100 ft); CAT III not applicable.

question: An operator calculates a CAT I DH of 170 ft from OCH plus margin. Which DH applies?

options.text: 230 ft
200 ft, the CAT I system minimum
185 ft, the average of the two values
170 ft

explanation: The system minimum overrides a lower calculated DH; for CAT I it is 200 ft. A calculated DH of 230 ft would stand, since it is higher.

question: In ILS procedure design, standard aircraft dimensions are assumed. For categories C and D, these are a wing span of 65 m and a vertical distance between wheels and glide path antenna of:

options.text: 8 m
6 m
7 m
3 m

explanation: Assumed dimensions: categories A/B 60 m span and 6 m; C/D 65 m and 7 m; DL 80 m and 8 m; helicopters 30 m and 3 m.

question: CAT II ILS operations are flown with:

options.text: A pressure altimeter only
A radio altimeter and a flight director
A head-up display only
A barometric DA referenced to QNH and a head-up display

explanation: CAT I is flown with the pressure altimeter; CAT II with radio altimeter and flight director.

question: The missed approach climb gradient normally assumed is:
explanation: The missed approach procedure is normally based on a 2.5% climb gradient.

question: ILS glide path angles are between:

options.text: 2.5° minimum and 3.5° maximum, with 3° required for CAT II/III
2° and 4°, with 3° required for CAT I
2.5° and 3°, with 2.5° required for CAT III and 3° preferred for CAT I approaches
3° and 3.5° in all cases

explanation: The glide path angle is between 2.5° and 3.5°; CAT II/III operations require 3°.

question: What is the optimum descent gradient for the final approach segment?

options.text: 3.3% (about 200 ft/NM)
6.5% (about 400 ft/NM)
2.5% (about 150 ft/NM)
5.2% (about 300 ft/NM)

explanation: The optimum final descent gradient is 5.2% (50 m/km, about 300 ft/NM), equivalent to a 3° path.

question: What is the maximum permissible descent gradient for a final approach (excluding special steep approaches)?

options.text: 9.5% (about 575 ft/NM)
8.0% (about 500 ft/NM)
6.5% (about 400 ft/NM)
5.2% (about 300 ft/NM)

explanation: The maximum is 6.5% (65 m/km, about 400 ft/NM), roughly a 3.7–3.8° path.

question: An approach has a glide path steeper than 6.5% (e.g. 5.5°). What approvals are needed?

options.text: Only the aircraft manufacturer's approval
State approval, an approved operator, specially approved aircraft and trained pilots
Only ATC approval on the day, and the pilot must announce the steep approach on first contact
None, if the pilot is informed

explanation: Steep approaches need specific approval from the State, approval of the operator, specially approved aircraft and specially trained pilots; they may not be used to avoid noise abatement procedures.

question: When is a track reversal procedure needed?

options.text: When straight-in is impossible and one facility is both IAF and MAPt
When the wind is above 20 kt
When the runway is too short for a straight-in landing
When the aircraft is above the MSA at the IAF

explanation: If a straight-in approach is not possible, a procedure using a facility on the aerodrome as both IAF and MAPt requires a track reversal (procedure turn or base turn).

question: A procedure turn is defined as a turn from outbound to inbound in which:

options.text: The aircraft turns through 180° over the facility
The outbound and inbound tracks are reciprocal
The inbound track is not the reciprocal of the outbound track
The turn is always made at rate 1 for 2 minutes

explanation: In a procedure turn the tracks are reciprocal. In a base turn they are not.

question: In a 45°/180° procedure turn, the straight leg after the 45° turn lasts how long for a Category C aircraft?

options.text: 1 minute 15 seconds
2 minutes
1 minute
1 minute 30 seconds

explanation: The leg after the 45° turn is 1 minute for Cat A and B, and 1 minute 15 seconds for Cat C, D and E, followed by a 180° turn to intercept at 45°.

question: An 80°/260° procedure turn consists of:

options.text: An 80° turn, a 1-minute leg, then a 260° turn in the same direction to intercept inbound
An 80° turn, then a 180° turn and a 1-minute leg
An 80° turn followed immediately by a 260° turn in the opposite direction
A 260° turn followed by an 80° turn in the same direction

explanation: The 80°/260° turn: a rate 1 turn of 80° followed immediately by a 260° turn in the opposite direction, ending on the reciprocal track.

question: A base turn differs from a procedure turn in that:

options.text: The outbound and inbound tracks are reciprocal
It is flown only with DME
It can only be used by Category A and B aircraft, as the turn radius is larger than a procedure turn
The inbound track is not the reciprocal of the outbound track

explanation: A base turn follows an outbound track to a point where a turn brings the aircraft onto an inbound track that is not the reciprocal of the outbound track.

question: A racetrack procedure is used when:

options.text: The aircraft is too fast for a holding pattern
The holding pattern orientation does not allow a procedure turn or base turn
No navaid is available for the approach
ATC needs to delay the aircraft by exactly 4 minutes before the start of the approach procedure

explanation: A racetrack (180° turn, outbound leg by time or fix, 180° turn inbound) is used where aircraft must enter a hold before the approach and its orientation does not permit a procedure or base turn.

question: When must a missed approach be flown?

options.text: Without the required visual reference at DA/H or MDA/H, or if unable to continue
When the RVR falls below the minimum at any point after the IAF
Only when the aircraft is below the glide path
Only when ATC instructs it

explanation: A missed approach is flown if the required visual reference is not obtained at DA/H or MDA/H, or at any time the pilot cannot continue the approach.

question: What does the published missed approach procedure always require?

options.text: An immediate turn towards the holding fix
A climb at maximum rate to the cruising level
A climb to at least the specified altitude, started as soon as the missed approach is begun
A level-off at MDA until the MAPt, then a climb at the best rate to the minimum sector altitude

explanation: The missed approach is always published (with the loss-of-RTF procedure) and includes a climb to at least a specified altitude, initiated as soon as the missed approach starts.

question: What are the three phases of a missed approach?

options.text: Initial, holding and return
Climb, cruise and descent
Go-around, acceleration and clean-up
Initial, intermediate and final

explanation: The missed approach consists of initial, intermediate and final phases.

question: Why are no turns specified in the initial phase of a missed approach?

options.text: The pilot is busy establishing the climb and changing configuration
Navaids cannot be received in this phase
ATC must give a clearance before any turn, and the controller is busy with the next arrival
Obstacles are always straight ahead

explanation: The initial phase begins at the MAPt and ends where the climb is established; the pilot is busy with climb and configuration, so no turns are specified.

question: Which is one way the missed approach point (MAPt) may be defined?

options.text: 1000 ft above the aerodrome elevation, measured on the pressure altimeter set to QFE
The outer marker
The intersection of the glide path with the DA/H
The initial approach fix

explanation: The MAPt may be the intersection of the glide path with the DA/H, a navaid, a fix, or a specified distance from the FAF.

question: A non-precision approach chart is annotated "timing not authorized for defining the MAPt". What does this mean?

options.text: The approach must be flown at maximum speed
The MAPt must be identified by a facility or fix, not by timing from the FAF
The approach cannot be flown without radar
The MAPt is defined only by the decision height, so the approach becomes a precision approach

explanation: Where timing is not to be used to locate the MAPt, the procedure carries this note; the MAPt is identified by its facility or fix.

question: A missed approach is started before reaching the MAPt. What should the pilot do?

options.text: Turn immediately onto the missed approach track
Climb straight ahead to the MSA and hold
Turn towards the holding fix by the shortest route, climbing to the published missed approach altitude
Proceed to the MAPt and then follow the missed approach procedure

explanation: The pilot should proceed to the MAPt (possibly higher than required) and then follow the missed approach procedure to stay within the protected airspace.

question: In the intermediate phase of a missed approach, the minimum obstacle clearance is:

options.text: 50 m throughout
90 m, until reaching the MSA
30 m, until 50 m (164 ft) clearance can be obtained and maintained
120 m, until the final phase starts at the minimum sector altitude for the aerodrome

explanation: In the intermediate phase the climb continues (turns up to 15° allowed) with 30 m MOC, until 50 m (164 ft) obstacle clearance is obtained and can be maintained.

question: The final phase of a missed approach begins where:

options.text: 50 m (164 ft) obstacle clearance is first obtained and can be maintained
The aircraft passes the MAPt
The aircraft reaches the MSA
The climb is first established and the configuration has been changed for the go-around

explanation: The final phase begins where 50 m (164 ft) obstacle clearance is first obtained and can be maintained, and extends to a new approach, holding or en route; full turns may be made.

question: Are aerodrome operating minima shown on State-published approach charts?

options.text: Yes, but only for circling approaches
No; setting them is the operator's responsibility
Yes, but only for CAT I approaches, as CAT II/III minima are set by the operator
Yes, for all categories

explanation: State charts (made to Annex 4) show OCA/H but not aerodrome operating minima, which the operator determines.

question: On an instrument approach chart, OCA/H values are shown:

options.text: Only for Category A aircraft
As a single value for all aircraft
Only for precision approaches, the non-precision values being left to the operator
For each aircraft category, for straight-in and circling approaches

explanation: Charts show OCA (OCH) for each aircraft category, e.g. for CAT I and CAT II ILS and for visual manoeuvring (circling).

question: An RNAV approach based on VOR/DME is classified as:

options.text: A non-precision approach
An approach with vertical guidance
A precision approach
A visual approach

explanation: VOR/DME RNAV procedures are non-precision; the reference facility is a VOR with co-located DME.

question: Before starting a flight with a VOR/DME RNAV approach planned, the operator must ensure that:

options.text: The approach chart has been checked by ATC
The aircraft has two GNSS receivers
The RNAV kit and the VOR/DME are serviceable and the pilot is current
A radar service is available at the destination

explanation: Before flight it must be ensured that the RNAV equipment is serviceable, the pilot knows how to operate it, and the published VOR/DME facility is serviceable.

question: Why are data insertion errors a concern in RNAV procedures?

options.text: The system rejects all manual entries
The VOR transmits corrections that may be lost
The data is updated automatically every hour, so manual entries are overwritten during the approach
The system cannot detect errors in data entered by the operator or crew

explanation: The computer must be programmed with current data inserted by the operator or crew; it has no way of checking for input errors, so its output may contain them.

question: Which factor affects the accuracy of a VOR/DME RNAV system?

options.text: The type of engines fitted
Distance from the reference facility
The aircraft's maximum take-off mass
The number of passengers on board

explanation: Accuracy depends on ground station tolerance, airborne receiver tolerance, flight technical tolerance, computational tolerance and distance from the reference facility.
